title: Problems have patterns
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Are you treating a symptom or the problem?

A student said: the symptoms against diagnosing the actual problem. Jose said: very good. Problems have patterns, and when you analyze patterns you get into if-then scenarios: if I do this, the outcome is this.
If-then problem solutions give us an idea of how we can solve problems, he said, and of coming up with alternative solutions.

Jose gave an example from his own company: we had a problem with a material we use to solve an erosion problem. The supplier has been going up and up in price. We believe that because they don't have a well-defined business model, they are trying to solve the problem by increasing the price of their product, which hurts our business in a particular area.

So how do we solve it? We solved it by becoming strategic about it, he said. Can we replace the material? What price can we get? Are we committing any patent infringement with a new material? We ask these questions to attack the problem.
We have to come up with a solution and not be dependent on buying the material from them, because it will eat into our margins, and we won't have a sustainable business model eventually.
What is the pattern behind the problem you keep solving?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a problem you keep solving.
Write the if-then that would change the outcome.
Write the dependency you want to remove.

check.q: What did a student contrast with diagnosing the problem?
What did Jose say effective problem solvers see?
What did Jose do about the supplier raising prices?
choices: Asked whether the material could be replaced and at what price

recap: Diagnose the problem, not the symptom. Look for the pattern. Ask if-then.
